title: Keep the cards, skip the chart
allegory: A factored matrix is keeping two decks of short profile cards instead of printing the giant chart of every pair's match score: any score is just two cards laid together, and the chart's main themes can be read off the small decks.
map: the giant chart of every pair's score
the full product M = AB, e.g. a 50k × 50k QK circuit
a deck of short cards, one per row
a deck of short cards, one per column
laying two cards together to get one score
one entry of M: a row of A dotted with a column of B
reading the chart's main themes off the small decks
SVD, norms and eigenvalues computed from the factors with small r-sized work

cap.1: You want to see which words a head links to which. The full table has 50,000 rows and 50,000 columns: about 2.5 billion numbers. It won't fit.
cap.2: A full QK circuit over GPT-2's vocabulary is 50k × 50k. Stored in float32 that is about 10 GB for one head, before you've computed anything about it.
cap.3: W_Eᵀ W_QK W_E is d_vocab × d_vocab, but it factors through d_head = 64, so its rank is at most 64. Materialising it wastes nearly all of its 2.5 × 10⁹ entries.

cap.1: But every number in that table is just two short cards laid together. Keep the two decks, 64 numbers per card, and make any entry on demand.
cap.2: M = AB with A (50k × 64) and B (64 × 50k). Storing A and B takes about 6.4 million numbers instead of 2.5 billion, and any entry is one row of A dotted with one column of B.
cap.3: A FactoredMatrix holds A and B separately; entry (i, j) is A[i]·B[:, j] and the product is never formed. Storage drops from d_vocab² to 2·d_vocab·d_head.

cap.1: Every card has only 64 numbers, so the giant table can only hold 64 independent patterns, however big it looks.
cap.2: A (50k × 64) times a (64 × 50k) matrix has rank at most 64, so at most 64 nonzero singular values. Everything interesting about it lives in a 64-dimensional space.
cap.3: rank(AB) ≤ min(rank A, rank B) ≤ d_head. The vocab-sized object is a low-rank bilinear form, so all of its spectral content is recoverable from r-sized computations.

cap.1: To find the table's main themes you never build the table. You do a little work on the two decks, then stitch the answers back together.
cap.2: Take the SVD A = U S Vᵀ, then the SVD of the thin matrix S Vᵀ B, and multiply the left factors back together. Eigenvalues come from the 64 × 64 matrix BA. This week's exercise derives properties like these.
cap.3: M = U_A(S_A V_Aᵀ B) = (U_A U′) S V′ᵀ, costing O(d_vocab·r²). Nonzero eigenvalues of AB equal those of BA. Frobenius norm = √Σσᵢ². No d_vocab² tensor ever exists.

chapters.name: Half the circuit
chapters.verdict: Score the whole path the stream receives, not one head.

cap.1: A real surprise from this week: one copying head's table scores only 30.79% on 'copies its input'. Add its twin head's table and it jumps to 95.6%.
cap.2: Heads 1.4 and 1.10 share an attention pattern, so the stream receives the sum of their OV circuits. Scored alone, 1.4 copies 30.79% top-1; the sum scores 95.6%. Score the whole path.
cap.3: The effective circuit is W_E(W_VW_O[1.4] + W_VW_O[1.10])W_U. It stays factored: place the factors side by side, rank ≤ 128. top_1_acc: 0.3079 alone, 0.956 summed.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Read a head as two small maps
Never build what you can keep factored
LoRA stores its update the same way

cap.1: Keeping giant tables as two small decks is what lets you read a whole head across the vocabulary on an ordinary machine, in seconds.
cap.2: FactoredMatrix is a TransformerLens library call: hold A and B, ask for svd, norm or eigenvalues. The habit carries into the grokking and OthelloGPT exercises, and LoRA stores its update this way.
cap.3: Weights-only circuit analysis, a first step in understanding and then steering a model, needs the spectra of vocab-sized low-rank maps. Factoring is what makes them computable at all.

coda.title: Paint a table and watch its rank: when do two decks beat the chart?

readouts.label: rank (independent patterns)
readouts.f: (M => { const A = M.map(row => row.slice()); const n = A.length, m = A[0].length; let rank = 0; for (let c = 0; c < m && rank < n; c++) { let p = -1; for (let i = rank; i < n; i++) if (abs(A[i][c]) > 1e-9) { p = i; break; } if (p < 0) continue; const t = A[rank]; A[rank] = A[p]; A[p] = t; for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) if (i !== rank) { const f = A[i][c] / A[rank][c]; for (let j = c; j < m; j++) A[i][j] -= f * A[rank][j]; } rank++; } return rank; })(G)

readouts.label: worth factoring?
readouts.f: (M => { const A = M.map(row => row.slice()); const n = A.length, m = A[0].length; let rank = 0; for (let c = 0; c < m && rank < n; c++) { let p = -1; for (let i = rank; i < n; i++) if (abs(A[i][c]) > 1e-9) { p = i; break; } if (p < 0) continue; const t = A[rank]; A[rank] = A[p]; A[p] = t; for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) if (i !== rank) { const f = A[i][c] / A[rank][c]; for (let j = c; j < m; j++) A[i][j] -= f * A[rank][j]; } rank++; } return rank; })(G) < 4 ? 'yes: the decks are smaller' : 'no: just store the table'

caption.1: This table is secretly one short list times another: rank 1. Tap squares to add patterns and watch the rank climb. Copy a row exactly and it won't move.
caption.2: Rank counts independent row patterns. A rank-r table can be stored as an (8 × r) deck times an (r × 8) deck: 16r numbers against 64. From rank 4 up, the decks stop being smaller.
caption.3: A rank-r n × n matrix factors as (n × r)(r × n), 2nr numbers. For a QK circuit n ≈ 50k and r ≤ 64, so factoring wins by a factor of n/2r ≈ 390.

where_else: LoRA: a weight update stored as two thin factors instead of a full matrix
Full QK and OV circuits for any head, and K-composition circuits between heads
The grokking and OthelloGPT exercises, which reuse the never-materialise habit

hamming.what: A big matrix kept as the two thin matrices it is the product of, with its properties computed from them.
hamming.when: Whenever a product is far bigger than its shared inner dimension, like a 50k × 50k circuit that factors through 64.
hamming.why: The product would not fit in memory, yet its entries, SVD, norms and eigenvalues are all recoverable cheaply from the factors.

object.title: The theme table
object.subtitle: A 10 × 10 table built from a few themes, each one short list down the side times one along the top.

cap.1: A 10 by 10 table made of one theme: one short list down the side times one along the top. Rank 1: 20 numbers describe all 100.
cap.2: A rank-1 matrix is an outer product u vᵀ: every row is a multiple of the same pattern.
cap.3: Rank 1: M = u vᵀ, storage 2n instead of n².

cap.1: Add a second theme, a slope rising along both edges. Still only two pairs of short lists.
cap.2: Adding a second outer product makes rank 2: M = u₁v₁ᵀ + u₂v₂ᵀ, still stored as two thin decks.
cap.3: Each rank-1 term adds one column to A and one row to B.

cap.1: A third theme digs a valley. Each theme is one card column in deck A and one card row in deck B.
cap.2: Three themes: A is 10 × 3, B is 3 × 10, 60 numbers for a 100-entry table.
cap.3: Rank 3 means a 3-dimensional row space; any row is a mix of three basis patterns.

cap.1: A fourth adds a fine checker. It looks busy, but it is four themes: 80 numbers as decks. With 50k rows and 64 themes, decks are about 390 times smaller.
cap.2: Rank 4 here costs 80 numbers against 100. At vocab scale, 50k × 64 decks beat a 50k × 50k table by n/2r ≈ 390.
cap.3: Savings scale as n/2r: negligible for tiny n, enormous for d_vocab ≈ 50k with r = d_head = 64.

cap.1: An SVD finds a table's strongest independent themes, strongest first. With the table kept as decks, it only ever needs the decks.
cap.2: SVD ranks the directions a matrix stretches most. FactoredMatrix computes it from A and B, never from M.
cap.3: Singular vectors of AB come from the SVD of A followed by the SVD of the thin S Vᵀ B: O(n·r²) instead of O(n³).

predict.q: A matrix is a (50k × 64) times a (64 × 50k). At most how many nonzero singular values can it have?
predict.why: A product's rank is at most its inner dimension, so the whole spectrum lives in 64 dimensions.

predict.q: Head 1.4's full OV circuit scores 30.79% on copying. What should you check first?

Conclude that head 1.4 does not copy

predict.q: How much smaller is a rank-64, 50k × 50k matrix when kept factored?

options.t: About 390 times: 6.4 million numbers instead of 2.5 billion

predict.why: Two 50k × 64 decks against one 50k × 50k table: n / 2r ≈ 390.
